extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students and researchers studying measure-theoretic probability (martingales, conditional expectation)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted section of a probability textbook covering regular conditional distributions, conditional expectation, definitions and basic properties of martingales, convergence theorems, inequalities, and several canonical examples and applications (Polya urn, Radon-Nikodym, branching processes). Useful for learning/proving results about martingales and applying them to probabilistic problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular conditional distribution (r.c.d.) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) For a.e. ω, ω → µ(ω, A) is a version of P(X ∈ A | G). (ii) For a.e. ω, A → µ(ω, A) is a probability measure on (S, S). When S = Ω and X is the identity map, µ is called a regular conditional probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the canonical definition used to represent conditional probabilities/expectations as kernels µ(ω,·). It emphasizes the two roles: for fixed A it is a version of the conditional probability; for fixed ω it is a probability measure on S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete r.c.d. from joint density (Example 4.1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y have joint density f(x,y)>0, define µ(y,A) = ∫_A f(x,y) dx / ∫ f(x,y) dx so that µ(Y(ω),A) is a r.c.d. for X given σ(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To check properties use taking h=1_A and dominated convergence to show A→µ(y,A) is a probability measure. Illustrates how ordinary conditional densities give regular conditional distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional expectation via r.c.d. (Theorem 4.1.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: If µ(ω,A) is a r.c.d. for X given F and f:(S,S)→(R,R) with E|f(X)|<∞ then E(f(X)|F) = ∫ µ(ω,dx) f(x) a.s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by showing case f=1_A from definition, extend by linearity to simple functions and monotone convergence for nonnegative f, then decomposition into positive/negative parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonexistence pathology of r.c.d.'s
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular conditional distributions do not always exist; Dieudonné (1948) provided the first example. The problem arises because exceptional null sets may 'pile up' when S contains enough countable collections of disjoint sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivates restricting to 'nice' measurable spaces (standard Borel) where existence is guaranteed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of r.c.d. for nice spaces (Theorem 4.1.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: r.c.d.'s exist if (S,S) is nice (i.e., there is a 1-1 measurable map ϕ:S→R with measurable inverse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: use ϕ to transfer to real line, construct distribution functions G(q,ω)=P(ϕ(X)≤q|G) as versions in ω, define F via inf of G(q,ω), get measures ν(ω,·) on R from F and pull back to S via ϕ; measurability checked using π-λ theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of measurable kernel µ(y,A) for σ(Y) (Theorem 4.1.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y take values in a nice space (S,S) and G = σ(Y), there is a function µ : S × S → [0,1] such that (i) for each A, µ(Y(ω),A) is a version of P(X∈A|G); (ii) for a.e. ω, A→µ(Y(ω),A) is a probability measure on (S,S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction similar to Theorem 4.1.17 but ensures µ depends measurably on y; uses representation G(q,ω)=H(q,Y(ω)) and π-λ theorem to verify measurability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bayes' formula (conditional version) (Exercise 4.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For G ∈ G, P(G|A) = ∫_G P(A|G) dP / ∫_Ω P(A|G) dP. When G is σ-field of a partition, reduces to usual Bayes formula: P(Gi|A) = P(A|Gi)P(Gi) / Σ_j P(A|Gj)P(Gj).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows equivalence between conditional probability kernels and standard Bayes when conditioning on partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional Chebyshev inequality (Exercise 4.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a>0 then P(|X| ≥ a | F) ≤ a^{-2} E(X^2 | F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A direct conditional version of Chebyshev; used to bound tail probabilities given sigma-field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (Exercise 4.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows by imitating standard proof with conditional expectation; foundational inequality for conditional L2 theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional Hölder inequality via r.c.d. (Exercise 4.1.4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive from unconditional Hölder using regular conditional distributions; useful for conditional Lp manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martingale / supermartingale / submartingale definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Given filtration Fn, a sequence Xn is adapted, E|Xn|<∞ and E(X_{n+1} | Fn) = Xn for all n then X is a martingale. Replace '=' by '≤' or '≥' to get supermartingale or submartingale respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core definition used throughout. 'Adapted' means Xn is Fn-measurable. Many examples and properties rely on this definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear martingale example (Example 4.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ξi i.i.d., Sn = S0 + ξ1 + ... + ξn, Fn = σ(ξ1,...,ξn). If µ = Eξi = 0, then Sn is a martingale; if µ ≤ 0 then Sn is a supermartingale (E(S_{n+1}|Fn) ≤ Sn), if µ ≥ 0 it's a submartingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows sums of independent increments with zero mean give martingales; subtracting mean produces martingale in nonzero-mean case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratic martingale (Example 4.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If µ=0 and σ^2 = Var(ξi) < ∞ then S_n^2 - nσ^2 is a martingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute via expansion and conditional independence. Useful for variance computations and stopping time arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exponential martingale (Example 4.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Yi≥0 i.i.d. with E Yi = 1 and Fn = σ(Y1,...,Yn), then M_n = ∏_{i≤n} Yi defines a martingale. In particular, Yi = exp(θ ξi)/φ(θ) has mean 1 and M_n = exp(θ S_n)/φ(θ)^n is a martingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard tool to produce martingales from cumulant generating functions; used in concentration and large deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supermartingale conditional monotonicity (Theorem 4.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xn is a supermartingale then for n>m, E(Xn | Fm) ≤ Xm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from the defining conditional inequality and repeated use of tower property; used to compare future expectations to current value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submartingale / martingale analogous conditional property (Theorem 4.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) If Xn is a submartingale then for n>m, E(Xn | Fm) ≥ Xm. (ii) If Xn is a martingale then for n>m, E(Xn | Fm) = Xm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows by applying Theorem 4.2.4 to -Xn or combining super/sub properties. Frequently invoked without proof in later results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convex transform of martingale is submartingale (Theorem 4.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xn is a martingale and φ is convex with E|φ(Xn)|<∞ then φ(Xn) is a submartingale. Consequence: if p≥1 and E|Xn|^p<∞, then |Xn|^p is a submartingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Jensen's inequality with conditional expectation. Provides a way to derive integrability and maximal inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing convex transform of submartingale (Theorem 4.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xn is a submartingale and φ is increasing convex with E|φ(Xn)|<∞ then φ(Xn) is a submartingale. Consequently (i) (Xn−a)^+ is a submartingale. (ii) If Xn is a supermartingale then Xn ∧ a is a supermartingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for truncation and upcrossing arguments; (X−a)^+ and truncations preserve (sub/super)martingale structure under mild conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable sequence and stochastic integral (H · X)
rubrics_metrics.description: A predictable sequence Hn satisfies Hn ∈ F_{n-1}. For adapted process Xn, define (H·X)_n = Σ_{m=1}^n Hm (Xm - Xm−1). Interpreted as gambling gains when Hm is amount wagered at time m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key object when studying betting strategies and optional stopping; predictable requirement enforces 'no peeking' at current increment before choosing Hn.

rubrics_metrics.name: No winning strategy for unfavorable game (Theorem 4.2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xn is a supermartingale and Hn≥0 are predictable bounded random variables, then (H·X)_n is a supermartingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that bounded predictable betting strategies cannot turn an unfavorable game (supermartingale) into a favorable one. Proof uses linearity of conditional expectation and the supermartingale inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stopping time and stopped process (Theorem 4.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If N is a stopping time and Xn is a supermartingale, then X_{N∧n} is a supermartingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses predictable indicator Hn = 1{N≥n} to express stopped process as stochastic integral plus constant and apply previous theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upcrossing inequality (Theorem 4.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xm is a submartingale and Un is number of completed upcrossings of [a,b] by time n, then (b−a) E Un ≤ E(Xn−a)^+ − E(X0−a)^+.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs truncated submartingale Y_m = a + (X_m − a)^+ and predictable H corresponding to trading strategy that captures at least (b−a) per upcrossing. Central to martingale convergence theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martingale convergence theorem (Theorem 4.2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xn is a submartingale with sup_n E X_n^+ < ∞ then Xn converges a.s. to a limit X with E|X|<∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses upcrossing inequality to show finiteness of upcrossings for rational a,b, hence limsup=liminf a.s.; Fatou's lemma gives integrability of limit. Fundamental result for almost-sure behavior of martingales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonnegative supermartingale convergence (Theorem 4.2.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xn ≥ 0 is a supermartingale then Xn → X a.s. as n→∞ and EX ≤ EX0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special case of martingale convergence applied to −Xn as submartingale; gives convergence without uniform integrability assumptions for nonnegative processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexamples: L1 convergence and probability vs a.s.
rubrics_metrics.description: Example 4.2.13: Nonnegative martingale X_n = S_{N∧n} converges a.s. to 0 but EXn = 1 for all n, so no L1 convergence. Example 4.2.14: Constructed Xk→0 in probability but not a.s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates limitations of convergence theorems (need stronger conditions for L1 convergence) and distinctions between convergence in probability and almost-sure convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded increments dichotomy (Theorem 4.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xn is a martingale with |X_{n+1}−X_n| ≤ M < ∞ then with probability 1 either lim Xn exists and finite or limsup Xn = +∞ and liminf Xn = −∞ (i.e., oscillates between ±∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses optional stopping on hitting large negative thresholds and Theorem 4.2.12 for stopped processes; describes qualitative behavior of bounded-step martingales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doob's decomposition (Theorem 4.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any submartingale Xn can be written uniquely as Xn = Mn + An where Mn is a martingale and An is a predictable increasing sequence with A0 = 0. Formula: An − An−1 = E(Xn | F_{n−1}) − X_{n−1}, so An = Σ_{m=1}^n E(Xm − Xm−1 | F_{m−1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive decomposition separating 'martingale part' and deterministic drift (predictable) part; used in many structural arguments and in proofs like Borel-Cantelli via martingales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator martingale example (Example 4.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given events Bn ∈ Fn, define M_n = Σ_{m=1}^n (1_{B_m} − E(1_{B_m} | F_{m−1})). Then M_n is a martingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic construction used to convert event sequences to martingales; used in upcrossing and Borel-Cantelli arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Borel-Cantelli lemma via martingales (Theorem 4.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For filtration Fn and events Bn∈Fn, {Bn infinitely often} = {Σ_n P(Bn | F_{n−1}) = ∞} a.s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct submartingale Xn = Σ_{m≤n} 1_{B_m} and its predictable compensator Σ P(Bm|F_{m−1}); apply Theorem 4.3.1 dichotomy to conclude equivalence. Provides conditional version of Borel-Cantelli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya's urn martingale and limit distribution (Section 4.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Polya urn with initial r red, g green, adding c balls of chosen color each draw, Xn = fraction of green balls is a martingale and Xn→X∞ a.s.; for c=1 the limit has Beta(g/c,r/c) density Γ((g+r)/c)/(Γ(g/c)Γ(r/c)) x^{g/c−1} (1−x)^{r/c−1}. Special cases give uniform distribution etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computations show Xn is martingale via conditional expectation on urn composition; limit distribution obtained by computing finite-sample combinatorial probabilities and taking n→∞.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radon-Nikodym derivative via martingales (Theorem 4.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given finite measure µ and probability ν, Fn ↑ F and µn<<νn with Xn = dµn/dνn and X = limsup Xn. Then µ(A) = ∫_A X dν + µ(A ∩ {X = ∞}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows Lebesgue decomposition and identification of Radon-Nikodym derivative as martingale limit; proof uses martingale convergence for Xn and decomposition with ρ=(µ+ν)/2 and π-λ arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kakutani dichotomy for product measures (Theorem 4.3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For product measures with coordinate densities q_n = dF_n/dG_n (assumed >0 G_n-a.s.), either µ<<ν or µ⊥ν according as ∏_{m=1}^∞ ∫ √{q_m} dG_m > 0 or = 0. Equivalently involves convergence of product of Hellinger integrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses martingale Xn = ∏_{m≤n} q_m(ω_m), analyze L^{1/2} norms and use Kolmogorov 0-1 law for tail event ν(X=0)∈{0,1} to deduce absolute continuity or singularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branching process martingale and extinction criteria (Lemmas/Theorems 4.3.9-4.3.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Galton-Watson with offspring mean µ, Z_n/µ^n is a martingale. If µ<1 then Z_n→0 a.s. (extinction) and Z_n/µ^n→0. If µ=1 and P(offspring=1)<1 then extinction occurs a.s. If µ>1 the extinction probability ρ is the smallest solution in [0,1) of ϕ(ρ)=ρ (ϕ generating function). Kesten-Stigum: limit W = lim Z_n/µ^n is nontrivial iff Σ p_k k log k < ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Martingale property used to deduce almost-sure limits; generating function iteration gives extinction probabilities; Kesten-Stigum gives sharp L^1/nontriviality condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation bounds at bounded stopping times (Theorem 4.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xn is a submartingale and N is a stopping time with P(N ≤ k)=1 then EX0 ≤ E X_N ≤ E X_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses that X_{N∧n} is submartingale and optional stopping for bounded times. Remarks note inequalities need not hold for unbounded stopping times without further conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doob's maximal inequality for submartingales (Theorem 4.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X_m be submartingale, X_n = max_{0≤m≤n} X_m, λ>0, A={X_n ≥ λ}. Then λ P(A) ≤ E X_n 1_A ≤ E X_n^+.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by stopping at first time exceeding λ (or at n), then applying Theorem 4.4.1; yields classical maximal inequalities e.g. Kolmogorov maximal inequality for sums by applying to X_n=S_n^2.
